_comment: THE NINE THIN SLOTS — the one thing a machine cannot close here.
Tier 0 is now the spine: 32 slots, one fixed English wording each, the same order in all twenty
languages. Every language fills what its sources can fill and reports the rest.
These slots fill in only one or two languages, because no Wikivoyage phrasebook carries them.
They cannot be filled from Tatoeba either, and the reason is worth writing down precisely, since
it is the third time this shape of trap has appeared in this project:
A keyword search matches WORD OVERLAP, not meaning. Searching Tatoeba for 'After you' returns
Hindi 'After cutting the vegetables, put them there' and Japanese 'Then simmer 30 minutes and
it's done' — both real sentences written by native speakers, both wrong for the slot. Searching
'My name is' returns Russian 'My BROTHER'S name is Tom' and Korean 'My GERMAN FRIEND's name is
Hans'. Roughly half the returned sentences do mean the slot, and nothing in the pipeline can
tell which half without a reader who speaks the language.
So these slots are LEFT EMPTY and reported by name on every build. Filling them by search would
ship about 85 entries whose meaning is wrong and whose provenance reads as native evidence — the
worst failure mode this project has, and one that would have to be deleted later.
What would close them, in order of cost:
1. A native speaker, or anyone who speaks the language, checking nine short phrases. This is
the real fix and it is small: nine phrases, not nine hundred.
2. Per-language authoring, labelled unverified. Better than nothing and better than a wrong
search result, but it means me writing languages Kedhar cannot check.
3. Leave them. The app shows the tier as it is, which is honest and costs a few slots.

measurement.filled: 345 of 640 slots across 20 languages (English 32/32, Japanese 19/32, Hindi 12/32)

parenthetical_in_native_text.status: OPEN — needs a policy decision, not a code fix
parenthetical_in_native_text.found: 2026-10-08, while reading Tier 1 fills rather than counting them
parenthetical_in_native_text.how: German 'I'm lost.' filled as "Ich habe mich verirrt. (eekh". A bracket rule caught the opening but not the truncated remainder, so the romanisation stayed inside text_native.
why_it_is_not_one_fix: The 224 are four different things, and stripping trailing parentheses would destroy two of them:
in text_romanized, which the linter requires anyway for a non-Latin script.
STAGE DIRECTION 'Jambo (response: Sijambo)' — belongs nowhere. It is the page talking.
REAL VARIANT    'le week-end (France) / la fin de semaine (Canada)' — two correct answers.
Stripping the parenthetical deletes a Canadian speaker's phrase.
PARSE ARTIFACT  'WC, Toilette(n)' — a broken tag left in the text. Unambiguous, fixable.
why_it_did_not_fail_the_linter: The linter requires a romanisation for a non-Latin script and it is satisfied — the text carries
one, just in the wrong field. In a Latin language there is no requirement at all, so a romanised
glue stays invisible. No rule in the linter can see this, and that is the point: it is a content
judgement, and only reading the output catches it.
parenthetical_in_native_text.cost_of_leaving_it: Tiers 1-3 ship lines with a pronunciation printed inside the phrase, and one corrupt '(n)'. Readable, and wrong in the way that erodes trust in the rest.
options: 1. Split the four classes apart with four explicit patterns and review the 224 by hand. Correct, and it is 224 lines of judgement I cannot do reliably without a reader.
2. Strip only the unambiguously-wrong ones (stage directions, romanisations in non-Latin scripts, parse artifacts) and leave regional variants. Roughly 110 rows fixed, 110 preserved.
3. Leave all 224 and document them. Honest, ships a known defect.

hindi_tier0_empty.status: OPEN — a language with no Tier 0, and it is one of the twenty
hindi_tier0_empty.measured: 2026-10-08: hin 0/32 Tier 0 slots, 17/55 Tier 1 slots, 17 entries total — the smallest language in the app by a factor of three
cause: The gate that refuses a non-Latin phrase with no reading is correct — a Devanagari line with no romanisation is unusable to the reader the app exists for. Hindi Tier 0 fills entirely from attested Tatoeba rows, and `loadAttested` sets pronunciation to null, so every candidate is held back and the tier is empty.
The Hindi Wikivoyage page has NO courtesy rows at all. Its twelve sections are Basics, Bus and Train, Directions, Taxi, Lodging, Money, Eating, Bars, Shopping, Driving, Problems, Authority.
So this is the nine-thin-slots problem at whole-tier scale: the captions do not exist in the sources, and Tatoeba cannot be searched for them safely.
why_not_worked_around: Relaxing the reading gate would ship Hindi entries no one can read. Filling from Tatoeba search would ship Hindi entries that are real sentences and wrong meanings. Neither is a fix; both are the failure this project exists to avoid.
what_would_fix_it: 1. Nine Hindi courtesy phrases in front of a speaker of Hindi. Same cost as the nine Tier 0 thin slots — a person, not a machine.
2. A romanisation source for Tatoeba sentences. None is in reach offline.
3. Accept it and say so in the app. Honest, and it is one language of twenty.

page_furniture_in_phrase_text.status: FIXED 2026-10-08 — rule added, verified on device
page_furniture_in_phrase_text.found: Reading the running app, not the data. German's FIRST Tier 0 card rendered as 'Hallo. (HAL-loo) NOTE: In Northern Germany, locals greet each other with Hello.' — the Wikivoyage editor's note to the reader of the web page, concatenated into the phrase with no delimiter and no bracket.
page_furniture_in_phrase_text.also: cmn: 'Example - 好不好？ （好不好？）' — a page label, the phrase, then the same phrase again.
page_furniture_in_phrase_text.why_no_linter_caught_it: The string is valid text in a valid field. There is no rule that can distinguish a phrase from a phrase with an editorial note welded to it; only reading the output catches it.
page_furniture_in_phrase_text.rule: `NOTE:` to end of string is cut; a leading 'Example - ' is cut. Both explicit and end-anchored. A note never ends mid-sentence and 'Example -' is only ever a prefix, so neither rule can cut into real content.

reviewer_checklist.status: LIVE — `catalogue/REVIEWER.md`, generated, with a working ingestion path
reviewer_checklist.size: 708 sentences across 87 slots, 20 languages. Tier 0: 292. Tier 1: 416.
why_not_634: The checklist first reported 634. That number was optimistic: it counted matches the assigner returned, including attested Tatoeba rows with no romanisation that the builder then refused. The measurement and the artefact disagreed, which is the same failure as the report claiming Hindi had 12 fillable slots on the run that shipped Hindi 0.

The reading requirement now lives inside assign(), the one function both the report and the builder call, so a slot can only be counted as fillable if it will actually ship. The number went UP to 708 because it is now true.
the_useful_unit_is_not_a_sentence: 708 sentences is not a job description. The list is ranked by how many LANGUAGES each slot is missing from, and that makes the work countable in slots rather than lines:
top  9 slots = 168 sentences   top 15 = 272   top 25 = 419   top 40 = 537

Nine slots closes a quarter of it. The top nine are the Tier 0 courtesy and repair slots that fill in one or two languages — the nine the search could not fill — plus the handful that Tatoeba happens to miss.
reviewer_checklist.ingestion: catalogue/reviewed/<lang>.jsonl, one object per line, {lang, slot, text_native, text_romanized, note, uncertain}. A reviewed row WINS every match, including over a harvested row whose caption fits better. An unknown slot id throws rather than loading a row that never matches, because a typo would otherwise look like it shipped.
reviewer_checklist.verified_end_to_end: One Hindi greeting row in the file moved Hindi Tier 0 from 0 to 1, shipped as `authored`, and disappeared when the row was removed. A deliberate typo (`greeting.helo`) was refused by name.
